summary: Summarizes the Workshop on Internet of Things Semantic Interoperability held in Santa Clara, California on March 17-18, 2016. It discusses the approaches companies and standards bodies use for IoT interoperability.

eli5.summary: Many companies make smart gadgets that speak different languages. Experts met to talk about how to get them to understand each other.

questions: how do iot devices from different vendors work together
what is an information model in iot
what is the difference between information and data models
subtitle: Bridging the language gap between smart devices from different vendors.

tldr.problem: The Internet of Things is fragmented: each standards organization and vendor uses different data formats, information models, and APIs for their devices, making them incompatible with each other.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB organized a 2016 workshop where experts from major IoT organizations explored how companies define and describe device behavior, and how to translate between different approaches to achieve interoperability.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified key problems, proposed solutions like a common translation hub and runtime discovery, and established collaboration channels for ongoing work between organizations.

today: RFC 8477 is an Informational IAB report documenting the workshop proceedings. Since 2016, the IoT landscape remains fragmented across standards, though increased attention to semantic interoperability and YANG-based approaches in various domains has built on the workshop's findings.

sections.title: The Interoperability Challenge
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) held a workshop on March 17-18, 2016 in Santa Clara, California to address a fundamental problem: as the Internet of Things expanded, each standards organization and company defined its own data formats and communication protocols, making devices from different vendors unable to work together.

The workshop gathered participants from major IoT players including the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA), Bluetooth SIG, Open Connectivity Foundation (OCF), AllSeen Alliance, World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), and the IETF. The goal was to explore how these groups approach interoperability at the application layer and to identify gaps that needed addressing.
sections.eli5: Different smart device makers use different instructions for their gadgets. Engineers from all the big companies met to understand each other's approaches and find ways to make everything work together.

sections.title: Three Key Concepts
sections.content:
The workshop established three distinct concepts that were often confused. An information model is the abstract blueprint of what a device can do, expressed informally (like plain English) or formally (like diagrams or formal languages). A data model is the concrete, implementation-specific definition of how that information is actually encoded and sent—examples include SNMP MIB modules, YANG modules, JSON Schemas, and XML representations.

An interaction model describes how software actually accesses and uses that data. The same information can be accessed through REST methods, publish-subscribe messaging, or Remote Procedure Call (RPC) style APIs. Many groups were not clearly separating these concepts, causing confusion and preventing compatibility.
sections.eli5: There are three levels: what a device can do in the abstract (information model), how that gets written down in code (data model), and how software actually talks to it (interaction model). Different companies were mixing these up.

sections.title: The Problems Identified
sections.content:
Workshop participants identified several root causes of fragmentation. Organizations use different formal languages to describe their models: OMA uses XML Schema, Bluetooth uses XML, OCF uses JSON Schema and RAML, AllSeen uses AllJoyn Introspection XML, W3C uses Resource Description Framework (RDF), and IETF uses YANG. Each language is optimized for its ecosystem.

Beyond formats, participants discussed that building gateways to translate between every pair of data models creates an explosion of complexity—in the worst case, n^2 - n different translators for n different systems. Debugging is hard without tools to browse and inspect device models at runtime. Device APIs evolve over time, but existing systems often require manual code changes to adapt rather than discovering new capabilities dynamically.
sections.eli5: Every company uses its own form for writing down how their devices work. To connect them all, you'd need a different translator for every pair of devices, which gets complicated fast. Also, when devices get new features, the client programs have to be rewritten by hand.

sections.title: Proposed Solutions
sections.content:
For translating between models, participants discussed the "red star" approach: instead of translating every system directly to every other system, translate all models to and from a common central model. This reduces translators needed from n^2 to 2n. The challenge is deciding what that central model looks like and whether one design can serve all use cases.

The workshop noted that translation can happen at design time (converting a YANG module to a JSON Schema once) or runtime (translating actual data values as they cross a bridge). Runtime discovery of device capabilities, where a client learns what a device can do by querying it rather than reading a static specification, offers more flexibility. Some systems like AllJoyn and approaches based on HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) demonstrate this possibility.
sections.eli5: One idea: instead of translating device A to B to C to D, translate everything to a middle language that everyone understands. Also, devices could tell clients what they can do when they connect, instead of the client guessing based on a manual.

sections.title: Security Across Ecosystems
sections.content:
Workshop participants observed that security models vary significantly between ecosystems. Different systems disagree on who the security principals are (users, devices, applications, or some combination), whether to use Access Control Lists or capability-based security, and what policies can be expressed. These differences make translation between systems complex because the translator must understand and convert between fundamentally different security assumptions.

Proposals included tagging data with privacy levels as metadata, allowing the translator to enforce privacy policies, or having the translator act as a trusted intermediary that understands both security models. The challenge is that sometimes even the privacy level of data is itself sensitive information.
sections.eli5: Different devices have different ideas about who is allowed to do what. When translating, the bridge has to understand both worlds and make safe choices about who gets access.

sections.title: Moving Forward Together
sections.content:
The workshop concluded with practical steps for collaboration. Participants created a shared GitHub repository and mailing list to share information about meeting schedules, allowing organizations to collocate their events. They discussed establishing a common repository for published data models to improve reuse.

The Open Connectivity Foundation's oneIoTa repository was suggested as a possibility for hosting schemas from multiple organizations, though licensing concerns existed at the time. The workshop acknowledged that terminology work would continue independently within each organization, and the community agreed to ongoing information sharing rather than attempting to impose a single standard.
sections.eli5: The groups decided to keep talking, share a list of their meetings and data models, and help each other understand what everyone is working on.
